q: Propene reacts with HBr in the gas phase to give 2-bromopropane. What are the signs of ΔH° and ΔS° for this reaction?
h: Count the molecules on each side, and compare the bonds broken (one π bond, one H–Br) with the bonds formed (two σ bonds).
w: An addition breaks a weak C=C π bond and the H–Br bond and makes two stronger σ bonds (C–H and C–Br), so heat is released: ΔH° < 0. Two gas molecules become one, so disorder drops: ΔS° < 0. ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0. Additions like this are favored at low temperature, where the −TΔS° penalty is small.
x: Two molecules combine into one, which lowers the entropy; ΔS° is negative, not positive.
Two σ bonds formed are stronger than the π bond plus H–Br bond broken, so the reaction is exothermic.
Both signs are reversed: this describes the reverse reaction, the elimination of HBr from 2-bromopropane.

q: The Diels–Alder reaction of 1,3-butadiene with ethylene has ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0. How does K<sub>eq</sub> for this reaction change as the temperature is raised?
c: K<sub>eq</sub> decreases, because the −TΔS° term becomes more unfavorable
K<sub>eq</sub> increases, because molecules collide more often at high temperature
K<sub>eq</sub> stays the same, because ΔH° and ΔS° do not depend on temperature
K<sub>eq</sub> increases, because the −TΔS° term becomes more favorable
h: Write ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. With ΔS° negative, what does a larger T do to the −TΔS° term?
w: With ΔS° < 0, the term −TΔS° is positive and grows with temperature, so ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° becomes less negative (and eventually positive). Since ΔG° = −RT ln K, a less negative ΔG° means a smaller K. Keq decreases with temperature, which is why the retro-Diels–Alder reaction takes over when these adducts are heated strongly.
x: Collision frequency affects the rate (how fast equilibrium is reached), not the position of equilibrium.
Even if ΔH° and ΔS° are constant, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° contains T, so K must change.
With ΔS° < 0, −TΔS° is positive; it grows more unfavorable, not more favorable, as T rises.

q: An equilibrium A ⇌ B at 25 °C (298 K) has K<sub>eq</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>. What is ΔG° for A → B? (R = 8.314 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K with the natural log, and keep the units of R in mind.
w: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314 J mol−1 K−1)(298 K)(ln 1000) = −(2478 J/mol)(6.91) = −17 100 J/mol = −17.1 kJ/mol. A handy rule: at 25 °C each factor of 10 in K is worth about 5.7 kJ/mol, and 3 × 5.7 = 17.1.
x: This uses log<sub>10</sub>(1000) = 3 instead of ln(1000) = 6.91; the equation needs the natural log.
K > 1 means products are favored, so ΔG° must be negative.
This is only −RT (2.48 kJ/mol); it leaves out the ln K factor.

q: For methylcyclohexane, ΔG° = −7.3 kJ/mol for the ring flip of chair I to chair II at 25 °C. About what percent of the molecules have the methyl group equatorial at equilibrium?
h: First find K from ΔG° = −RT ln K (watch kJ vs J), then turn K = [II]/[I] into a fraction.
w: K = e−ΔG°/RT = e7300/(8.314 × 298) = e2.95 ≈ 19. In chair II the methyl is equatorial, so the fraction equatorial = K/(1 + K) = 19/20 = 95%.
x: This comes from using 10<sup>2.95</sup> instead of e<sup>2.95</sup>; ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log.
This results from dividing 7.3 (kJ) by RT in J (2478), which gives K ≈ 1; convert ΔG° to 7300 J/mol first.
This is the axial percentage: a negative ΔG° for I → II favors chair II, which has the methyl equatorial.

q: The SN2 reaction CH3I + CH3S− → CH3SCH3 + I− in DMF follows rate = k[CH3I][CH3S−]. If [CH3I] is tripled and [CH3S−] is halved, the initial rate becomes
h: Multiply the factor for each concentration by its order in the rate law.
w: Both reactants appear to the first power, so the rate changes by (3)(½) = 1.5.
x: A factor of 3 ignores the change in [CH<sub>3</sub>S<sup>−</sup>]; the reaction is first order in the nucleophile too.
A factor of 6 multiplies by 2 for the nucleophile instead of by ½.
A factor of 0.5 ignores the tripling of [CH<sub>3</sub>I], which also appears in the rate law.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with NaN<sub>3</sub> in aqueous acetone by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. If [alkyl bromide] is halved and [N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] is doubled, the initial rate
h: Which species are present in the rate-determining step of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction?
w: The rate-determining step of SN1 is ionization of the C–Br bond, so rate = k[RBr]; azide is not in the rate law. Halving [RBr] halves the rate, and doubling [N3−] has no effect.
x: Unchanged would be right for rate = k[RBr][N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] (an S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law), where ½ × 2 = 1.
Doubling assumes the rate depends only on azide; azide attacks after the slow step and does not appear in the rate law.
One-quarter treats the reaction as second order in RBr; S<sub>N</sub>1 is first order in substrate.

q:
Which changes increase the rate constant k (not just the rate) of a reaction?
I. Raising the temperature
II. Increasing the concentration of a reactant
III. Adding a catalyst that provides a lower-energy pathway
h: The Arrhenius equation, k = A e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>, contains no concentration term.
w: From k = A e−Ea/RT, k grows when T rises (I) or when Ea falls, which is what a catalyst does (III). Concentration changes the rate (rate = k[...]) but not k itself. I and III only.
x: Concentration (II) changes the rate through the rate law, but k is a constant at a given temperature.
II changes the rate, not k; and I and III do change k.
A catalyst lowers Ea, which also increases k, so III belongs with I.

q: How many transition states and how many intermediates are shown in this reaction energy diagram?
h: Transition states are maxima; intermediates are local minima between maxima. Reactants and products are not intermediates.
w: The maxima A and C are transition states, and the valley B between them is an intermediate. 2 transition states and 1 intermediate, so this is a two-step reaction.
x: This swaps the definitions: maxima (A, C) are transition states and the minimum (B) is the intermediate.
Reactants and products are not transition states or intermediates; only A, B and C count.
There is only one valley between the two peaks; reactants and products are not intermediates.

q: Which step of the reaction in this energy diagram is rate-determining, and why?
c: Step 2, because its transition state C is the highest-energy point on the path
Step 1, because its barrier (reactants to A) is larger than the barrier from B to C
Step 1, because it is endothermic while step 2 is exothermic
Step 2, because exothermic steps are always slower than endothermic steps
h: Intermediate B lies above the reactants and can fall back over A easily. What is the highest point every molecule must pass?
w: Every molecule that becomes product must pass C, the highest point on the diagram (20 units above the reactants). Intermediate B can return over A (barrier 4) more easily than it goes on over C (barrier 10), so B and the reactants equilibrate and the overall barrier is reactants → C. Step 2 is rate-determining because C is the highest transition state.
x: Comparing individual barriers misleads here: B lies above the reactants, so the overall barrier to product is reactants → C (20), larger than 14.
Whether a step is endothermic does not decide the rate-determining step; the highest transition state does.
Step 2 is the right step, but the reason is wrong: exothermic steps are not slower in general; C is simply the highest point.

q: The first step of the S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a strongly endothermic ionization. According to the Hammond postulate, the transition state of this step most resembles
c: the tert-butyl cation and bromide ion
an equal blend of the alkyl bromide and the substitution product
h: The Hammond postulate says a transition state resembles the species (reactant or product of that step) closest to it in energy.
w: For an endothermic step the transition state lies close in energy to the higher-energy side, the products of that step. Here those are (CH3)3C+ and Br−, so the TS is late and has much carbocation character: it resembles the tert-butyl cation and bromide. That is why factors that stabilize the cation speed up SN1 reactions.
x: An early, reactant-like TS goes with an exothermic step; this ionization is endothermic.
The Hammond postulate compares a TS with the reactant and product of that one step; the final product forms in a later step.
A TS halfway between is expected only for a thermoneutral step; this step is strongly uphill.

q: Radical bromination of propane gives about 97% 2-bromopropane, while chlorination gives only about 55% 2-chloropropane. Which explanation uses the Hammond postulate correctly?
c: H abstraction by Br• is endothermic, so its transition state is late, resembles the alkyl radical and feels the stability difference between 2° and 1° radicals
H abstraction by Br• is exothermic, so its transition state is early and resembles propane, which makes it more selective
Br• is more reactive than Cl•, so it attacks the more crowded 2° hydrogens more often
H abstraction by Cl• is endothermic, so its transition state is late and cannot tell 2° from 1° hydrogens apart
h: Compare the H–Br and H–Cl bond strengths with a C–H bond to decide which abstraction step is uphill.
w: H–Br (366 kJ/mol) is weaker than a C–H bond (about 410–420 kJ/mol), so H abstraction by Br• is endothermic; H–Cl (431 kJ/mol) is stronger, so abstraction by Cl• is exothermic. An endothermic step has a late, product-like TS with nearly formed radical character, so the 2° radical's extra stability lowers its TS a lot. The late TS for bromination makes it selective. The early TS for chlorination resembles propane and shows little preference.
x: Abstraction by Br• is endothermic, not exothermic; and an early, reactant-like TS would make a reaction less selective.
Br• is less reactive than Cl•; lower reactivity (a later TS) goes with higher selectivity.
Abstraction by Cl• is exothermic with an early TS; that is why chlorination is unselective.

q:
Which statements about the reaction shown in this energy diagram are true?
I. There are two intermediates.
II. The overall reaction is endothermic.
III. The second step is rate-determining.
h: Count the valleys between peaks, compare products with reactants, and find the highest peak.
w: There are three peaks (transition states) and two valleys between them (energies 5 and 9): two intermediates, so I is true. Products lie below reactants, so the reaction is exothermic and II is false. The highest peak (18) is the second transition state, so step 2 is rate-determining and III is true. I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the second peak is the highest point on the diagram.
Statement II is false: the products end below the reactants, so the overall reaction is exothermic.
Statement I is true and II is false; the products lie below the reactants.

q: Which labeled atom in acetyl chloride is the most electrophilic site, the atom a nucleophile attacks?
h: Look for the atom with the largest partial positive charge, bonded to more than one electronegative atom.
w: The carbonyl carbon is bonded to both O and Cl, which pull electron density away, and resonance (C+–O−) puts a positive charge on it. Atom b, the carbonyl carbon, is the electrophile; nucleophiles add there in acyl substitution.
x: The methyl carbon carries little positive charge and has no leaving group or π bond; it is not electrophilic.
The oxygen is electron-rich (δ−, lone pairs); it is a nucleophilic/basic site, not an electrophilic one.
Chlorine is δ− and holds lone pairs; it leaves as chloride but is not where a nucleophile attacks.

q: In the first step of the addition of HBr to propene, a carbocation forms. Which statement identifies the nucleophile and electrophile in that step?
c: The C=C π bond is the nucleophile; the H of HBr is the electrophile
The Br of HBr is the nucleophile; an alkene carbon is the electrophile
The H of HBr is the nucleophile; the C=C π bond is the electrophile
The C=C π bond is the nucleophile; the Br of HBr is the electrophile
h: Electrons flow from the electron-rich site to the electron-poor atom. Which atom of H–Br is δ+?
w: The π electrons of the alkene attack the δ+ hydrogen of HBr, and the H–Br bond electrons leave with bromide. The π bond is the nucleophile and the H is the electrophile. Bromide acts as the nucleophile only in the second step, when it attacks the carbocation.
x: This describes the second step (bromide attacking the cation), and it is bromide ion, not HBr, that attacks.
This reverses the electron flow: the H of HBr is δ+ and electron-poor, so it accepts electrons.
The Br in HBr is δ−; the alkene bonds to the H, which is the δ+ atom, and Br leaves as bromide.

q: Rank these carbocations from most stable to least stable.
h: Alkyl groups stabilize a cation by hyperconjugation and induction. A vinyl cation has its positive charge on an sp-hybridized carbon.
w: More alkyl groups give more hyperconjugation, so 3° (I) > 2° (II) > 1° (III). The vinyl cation (IV) puts the charge on an sp carbon, which holds electrons tightly (50% s character), and the empty p orbital lies in the plane of the π bond, so the π bond cannot donate into it. Vinyl cations are even less stable than primary cations. I > II > III > IV.
x: A vinyl cation is not stabilized by its π bond (the empty orbital is perpendicular to it) and is less stable than a primary cation.
A vinyl cation is not allylic; its π bond cannot delocalize the charge, so it does not rank first.
The vinyl cation, not the primary cation, is the least stable; it does not rank above the 2° and 1° alkyl cations.

q: Rank these secondary carbocations from most stable to least stable.
h: Ask whether the neighboring atom can donate a lone pair into the empty p orbital, or instead withdraws electron density.
w: In I, an oxygen lone pair donates into the empty p orbital (resonance form C=O+–CH3 where every atom has an octet), a strong stabilization that outweighs oxygen's inductive pull. II is an ordinary 2° alkyl cation. In III the carbonyl group next to the cationic carbon withdraws electrons (its carbon is δ+), destabilizing it. I > II > III.
x: Oxygen's inductive withdrawal is outweighed by lone-pair donation (resonance), so I is more stable than II.
The carbonyl in III cannot donate electrons to the cation; its δ+ carbon makes III the least stable.
I is the most stable, not the least: the oxygen lone pair gives a resonance form with full octets.

q: 3-Methyl-2-butanol reacts with concentrated HBr to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product. Which carbocation is attacked by bromide to form this product?
h: The first cation forms where the OH was. Is there a hydrogen on a neighboring carbon whose shift would make the cation more substituted?
w: Loss of water from the protonated alcohol gives a 2° cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 (which carries one H and two methyls) moves the positive charge to C3, giving the more stable 3° cation. Bromide then attacks the 3° carbon, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: This is the first-formed 2° cation; bromide attacking it would give 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, not the observed product.
This is a 2° cation on an unbranched chain; no 1,2-shift turns a branched skeleton into a straight one.
This is a primary cation; hydride shifts go toward more stable cations, never from 2° to 1°.

q: 3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanol is heated with HCl. The first-formed carbocation undergoes a 1,2-shift. Which carbocation does that shift produce?
h: The carbon next to the cationic center has no hydrogen. What group can migrate from it instead?
w: Loss of water gives the 2° cation (CH3)3C–CH+–CH3. The neighboring quaternary carbon has no H, so a 1,2-methyl shift moves a CH3 with its bonding electrons to the cationic carbon, leaving a 3° cation (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Chloride then gives 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane.
x: This is the unrearranged 2° cation that forms first, not the product of the shift.
This is a primary cation; a hydride shift from a methyl group to the cation would trade a 2° cation for a less stable 1° one.
D has a different carbon skeleton (3-methylpentane); a single 1,2-methyl shift keeps the 2,3-dimethylbutane skeleton.

q: When 1-cyclobutylethanol is treated with HBr, the 1-cyclobutylethyl cation forms first. A ring C–C bond then migrates to the cationic carbon. Which carbocation is produced directly by that migration?
h: Follow the atoms: the ring carbon attached to the cationic carbon loses one ring bond, and the cationic carbon becomes a ring member. Where is the positive charge left?
w: In the alkyl shift, a ring C–C bond on the carbon next to the cation moves to the cationic carbon. The former exocyclic carbon (with its CH<sub>3</sub>) becomes part of a five-membered ring, and the positive charge is left on the old ring carbon next to it. The product is the 2-methylcyclopentyl cation: still 2°, but the 4-membered ring strain is relieved. A later 1,2-hydride shift can turn it into the 3° 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, which is how 1-bromo-1-methylcyclopentane forms.
x: This is formed only after a second step (a hydride shift from A); it is not the direct product of the ring bond migration.
C would come from a hydride shift without ring expansion; it keeps the strained four-membered ring.
D would require the methyl carbon to enter the ring too; only the cationic carbon joins the ring, so the ring grows from 4 to 5, not 6.

q: A reaction can give two products, P and Q. At low temperature and short reaction time it gives mostly P; after long heating it gives mostly Q. Which statement is correct?
c: P forms through the lower-energy transition state, and Q is the more stable product
P is the more stable product, and Q forms through the lower-energy transition state
P and Q form through the same transition state but differ in stability
Q forms faster, and P is the more stable product
h: Under kinetic control the product ratio reflects relative rates; under thermodynamic control it reflects relative product stabilities.
w: At low temperature the products cannot revert, so the faster-forming product (lower ΔG‡) dominates: kinetic control favors P. With heating and time, the reactions become reversible and the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product: thermodynamic control favors Q. P has the lower-energy transition state; Q is the more stable product.
x: This reverses the two kinds of control: the product formed at low temperature is the kinetic (faster) one.
Different products form through different transition states; that difference is what allows kinetic control.
Q dominates only after equilibration; it is the more stable product, while P is the one formed faster.
